question: How do silence and sudden loud chords build a character in music?
intro: Polichinelle is Punch, the puppet, and this 1923 Victor record is the only issued disc of it that he made. Hear the jerky opening gestures, the smooth Agitato that interrupts them, and the return of the heavy chords.

sections.label: Allegro vivace · puppet gestures and chords
Agitato · triplets over long bass notes
Opening gestures return · approximate
sections.mNote: opening gestures return at ppp, then loud chords close

cues.title: Fragments, then chords
cues.text: The Allegro vivace moves like a puppet: isolated fff notes, ppp flurries with grace notes, and silences. By about 0:25 the music has opened into ff chords in both hands, the first loud stretch.
cues.evidence: The score’s first page shows Allegro vivace, fff single notes, ppp grace-note figures and ff chords from the third system (https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/morceaux-de-fantaisie/polichinelle-op-3-4.htm). The analysis shows 1.4–2.2 attacks per second in the first 20 s, then level rising from −16.5 dB (0:15) to −9.6 dB (0:25) with 4.6 attacks per second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A title from a tenor
cues.text: The tenor Mikhail Slonov, a friend, suggested the name Polichinelle. It was one of the pieces added to the C♯ minor Prelude to make a set for a Kharkov concert in December 1892. Gutheil published all five in February 1893, dedicated to Arensky.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker’s note for Hyperion CDA66081 gives Slonov’s suggestion, the Kharkov concert, Gutheil’s publication in February 1893 and the dedication: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: A destroyed first attempt
cues.text: Victor’s ledger shows a first take on 20 October 1920 at Camden, destroyed. Rachmaninoff returned on 6 March 1923 in New York; take 2 was issued on Victor 74807, and on 6452 with Chopin’s F♯ major Nocturne.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix C-24643 lists take 1 (20 October 1920, Camden, destroyed) and take 2 (6 March 1923, New York) as master, with issues on Victor 74807 and 6452: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700009866/C-24643-Polichinelle_op._3_no._4 and https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/object/detail/41140/Victor_6452

cues.title: The Agitato begins
cues.text: Attacks fall below one a second around 1:25, then at about 1:34 the Agitato begins: smooth triplet figures, each group starting on an accented note, over long held bass notes. The spiky first section is gone.
cues.evidence: The score shows rests at the end of the first section and then Agitato with accented triplet groups over whole-note basses on pages 4–5. The analysis shows 0.4–0.8 attacks per second at 1:25–1:30 (level −25.2 dB at 1:30), a boundary of 0.66 at 1:34 and attacks back at 2.0 per second by 1:35.

cues.title: The phrase restarts
cues.text: The Agitato phrase is stated three times. The first two end in quiet held notes, and each is followed by a louder restart. In this record the level dips at 1:50 and 2:15 and recovers by about 2:00 and 2:25.
cues.evidence: Pages 4–6 of the score show the Agitato phrase restarting twice at f, after pp held notes. The analysis shows −28.5 dB at 1:50 recovering to −14.9 dB at 2:00, and −25.8 dB at 2:15 recovering to −11.1 dB at 2:25; boundaries fall at 1:50 (0.38), 2:02 (0.42), 2:14 (0.95) and 2:26 (1.00). The restart times are approximate.

cues.title: Chords struck like blows
cues.text: Near 2:25 the third restart builds into sfff chords, mostly in the left hand and cut off by rests, while the right hand keeps its running figures above. This is one of the loudest stretches of the record, and the strongest boundary falls at 2:26.
cues.evidence: Page 6 of the score shows an f restart of the Agitato and then sfff chords, chiefly in the left hand with rests, under continuing right-hand figures. The analysis shows the strongest boundary (1.00) at 2:26 and levels of −11.1 and −9.4 dB at 2:25 and 2:30.

cues.title: Taking the piece apart
cues.text: The RCA booklet quotes Rachmaninoff on his method: “You must take the work apart, peer into every corner, before you can assemble the whole.” It adds that he shaped each piece around one climax, or “point”, towards which the music rises and from which it recedes.
cues.evidence: Francis Crociata’s essay “The Composer” in the RCA/BMG booklet (1992) gives the quotation and the account of his interpretative method, linking it to Chaliapin: https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992. The booklet does not say where it locates the point of this piece, and no claim is made about it here.

cues.title: Detached chords at the end
cues.text: The last page returns to ff chords and fast runs, then ends on short fff chords separated by rests, with a fermata on the final rest. In this record the loud stretch runs from about 2:55 to 3:30 and the sound has stopped by 3:35.
cues.evidence: The score’s eighth page shows runs and a closing sequence of fff staccato chords with rests, ending on a rest with a fermata. The analysis shows levels of −8.0 to −10.6 dB from 2:55 to 3:25, −16.7 dB at 3:30 and silence at 3:35.

transitions.title: Loud chords fall silent, then triplets
transitions.how: The first section dies away into rests: attacks fall to under one a second and the level drops by about fifteen decibels between 1:20 and 1:30. Agitato then replaces the spiky, staccato writing with smooth triplet figures, each group starting on an accented note, above long held bass notes. Articulation, texture and character change together, and the new section is built on restating one phrase rather than on the opening’s fragments.
transitions.evidence: The score shows rests at the close of the first section and Agitato on page 4. The analysis shows level −10.0 dB at 1:20 and −25.2 dB at 1:30, 0.4–0.8 attacks per second at 1:25–1:30, and a boundary of 0.66 at 1:34.

transitions.title: Sfff chords, then the puppet returns
transitions.how: The third Agitato statement builds into sfff chords, chiefly in the left hand and cut off by rests, under continuing right-hand figures. Then the opening’s gestures come back at ppp: grace-note flurries and isolated staccato notes, followed by ff chords as at the start. Dynamics, articulation and texture all change at once, and the music recalls the first section rather than the Agitato.
transitions.evidence: Page 6 of the score shows sfff chords followed by ppp grace-note figures and, on page 7, ff chords. The analysis shows the strongest boundary (1.00) at 2:26, then level falling from −9.4 dB at 2:30 to −17.1 dB at 2:40 and attacks from 2.0 to 1.6 per second between 2:35 and 2:40. The time of the return, near 2:38, is estimated from the score and is not a detected boundary.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Victor 6452, recorded 1923).
fields.note: DAHR’s catalogue record for Victor 6452 gives a publication date of [1923], a catalogue-derived year rather than a release day. The 1925 Victor catalogue lists “In F Sharp Major (Op. 15, No. 2) and Polichinelle — Piano — Rachmaninoff”, which establishes publication no later than 1925 independently of the session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky

Ivanovka near Tambov · Dresden · New York · Villa Senar, Lake Lucerne · Beverly Hills

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
